newsitem.title: USA: Archer Daniels to plead guilty in price-fix case.
newsitem.headline: Archer Daniels to plead guilty in price-fix case.

text.p: Archer Daniels Midland Co. said Monday it agreed to plead guilty to federal charges related to price-fixing and pay fines totalling $100 million.

ADM said the agreement, which is subject to court approval, settles the Justice Department's investigation of price-fixing of feed additive lysine and citric acid, and closes a third investigation related to high-fructose corn syrup.

ADM said it will pay a fine of $70 million in connection with its plea in lysine, a feed additive used in poultry and swine feed, and $30 million in connection with citric acid, an organic acid used in various foods, beverages and other products.

ADM said the agreement constitutes a global resolution of all matters between Justice and ADM. The agreement also brings to a close federal investigations of alleged misconduct by ADM, including the government's investigation of the high fructose corn syrup product line.

The antitrust probe of alleged price-fixing in the food and feed additive markets was first disclosed by ADM in late June 1995. At that time, ADM said it was subpoenaed for documents and testimony as part of a probe of lysine, citric acid and high fructose corn syrup.
ADM said the plea agreement is the result of negotiations between the Justice Department and a special committee of its board of directors, comprised of seven independent board members.
ADM said the special committee was created in 1995 to respond to the Justice Department's investigation into ADM's alleged anti-competitive activity and related civil litigation.
ADM said the special committee believes the consensual, global resolution with the Justice Department is in the best interests of ADM's shareholders and the company.

While the plea agreement settles Justice's antitrust probe gainst ADM, it is not known if Justice plans to bring charges against two company executives. In its final proxy statement in advance of its Oct. 17 annual meeting, ADM said indictments in the lysine probe were being considered against the company and Michael Andreas, vice chairman, and Terrance Wilson, group vice president in charge of corn refining.
Andreas is also the son of ADM Chairman Dwayne Andreas.
ADM did not return a phone call requesting comment. The Justice Department was closed for the Columbus Day holiday and officials were unavailable.

A former ADM executive, Mark Whitacre, acted as a government informant for about three years in the antitrust probe. Whitacre, who was president of ADM's BioProducts Division, was fired in August 1995 when the company accused him of stealing $9.5 million.
